chapter_theme: Vijayan shows Tivittan the gods' hill and its play, points to the blood of the lion Tivittan has killed and praises the prince's duty to risk his body for the world's creatures and the form of fame that outlasts it, and the two then enter a scorching desert.

cast.role: the elder prince, called the conch-hued and the white-wave-hued, who shows and speaks
the younger prince, called the sea-hued, who killed the lion

758.reading: The speaker points to a hill-rock of emerald hung with white flowers and pollen, humming with bees, beside a pool thick with white lotus.

759.reading: The speaker says these shining places are where the dark-haired, crescent-toothed women of the sura race live.

760.reading: The speaker says the high-breasted women with gold ornaments who live in the brimming pool are the water-women.

761.reading: The speaker says the nagas' women bathe in the mountain pools, which swell and wash the gem rocks.

762.reading: The speaker says the lotus-eyed women who live with their lovers on the cool slopes are gandharva women, made of the nectar of song.

763.reading: The speaker says the silver mansions of the hill are the dwellings of Vidyadhara women and yakshis, and the whole town laughs in gold.

764.reading: The speaker points to the crystal halls with coral pillars where gods play with their consorts.

765.reading: The speaker says the gem-bright mansions and picture halls with jewelled gates are the dwellings of the gods.

766.reading: The speaker says the hill itself plays a drama, with wind through beetle-bored bamboo as flute, clouds as drum and peacocks as dancers.
766.nuance: கீசகம் is taken as bamboo that wind makes a flute of; the line is hard to construe and the sense of the first two lines is a guess.

767.reading: The poet says that after the speaker had shown the sea-hued prince these sights and said such things, they went on.
767.nuance: Grammar of lines 2 to 3 is loose; the conch-hued one is taken as the speaker and the sea-hued as the one shown, as the brothers are named in 778.
767.event: Vijayan shows Tivittan the sights of the hill and the two move on.

768.reading: The poet says that, having shown the hill of bees and flowering trees for the spear-bearer's delight, the speaker reached the end of a league and began to speak.
768.nuance: Who is meant by the one with the angry spear is not fixed; he is taken as Tivittan.
768.event: Vijayan shows Tivittan another hill, walks a league and begins to speak.

769.reading: The speaker points to the stream of blood running down from where the lion had come out of its cave, like red clay that the hill has vomited.
769.nuance: The verse is the fruit of the astrologer's word of soolamani 409, that within a month Tivittan would split a lion's mouth; here the deed is already done and seen only as blood.
769.event: Vijayan points out the blood of the lion that Tivittan killed.

770.reading: The speaker says the lion that swallowed lives and saw the world as trembling was beyond even the gods, so none but Tivittan could have destroyed it.

771.reading: The speaker says that when Tivittan raged he watched from afar and took it for illusion, and wondered when the roaring stream of blood came down the slope and proved it real.
771.nuance: மாயமா மதித்து நின்றேன் may mean he took it for illusion, or for a marvel; the first is followed.
771.event: Vijayan watches Tivittan's rage and the stream of blood after he kills the lion.

772.reading: The speaker says Tivittan killed the lion that had eaten the herds of elephants, so that from this day the whole world sleeps in peace.
772.nuance: The Jain work praises a killing; the verse justifies it by the lion's own killing and the safety it brings, and does not weigh it against non-killing.
772.event: Tivittan killed the lion that preyed on the elephant herds.

claims.claim: killing a beast that preys on others lets the world rest in safety

773.reading: The speaker says that when living beings are in danger, strong-armed princes do not weigh their own lives, for the king's sons have no duty beyond guarding the world.

claims.claim: a king's son's chief duty is to relieve the danger of living beings without counting his own life

774.reading: The speaker says that if the body cannot help the learned, the pious, the helpless, the ascetics and the brahmins when trouble falls on them, it brings no fruit, king.
774.nuance: மன்னா is the address; whether it names Tivittan or turns to a general king is not clear. The first line's list of kinds of people is also hard to divide.

claims.claim: a body that does not help others in their trouble yields no fruit

775.reading: The speaker says a man who lives on while watching beings suffer has the manliness of a eunuch's beauty, and that people like Tivittan, who offer even themselves to end the world's pain, stand on earth.
775.nuance: அலிபெற்ற அழகு is the verse's own measure of the man who lives on; line 3 reads எனையான் as 'myself' and line 4 as praise of Tivittan.

claims.claim: manliness lies in giving oneself to end the suffering of living beings, and living on while they suffer is empty

776.reading: The speaker says a person has two forms, the one of flesh and sinew that vanishes here and the other of fame that outlasts it and is praised by the world.
776.nuance: யாக்கை in line 3 is taken as the other body of fame; ஊழ் காத்து வந்து may mean the body is kept by fate until its time, but the clause is hard to construe.

claims.claim: the body of flesh passes but the form of fame remains after death

777.reading: The poet says that, having said this, the two went with the mace through a cloud-hill forest of flowers into a fierce desert, where the sun stood at noon and scorched the earth.
777.nuance: தங்கதை is taken as தம் கதை, their mace, the line is not secure.
777.event: The two princes enter a scorching wasteland at noon.

778.reading: The poet says that after they reached the desert, the white-wave-hued prince bade the sea-hued one see how this fierce forest was.
778.nuance: Line 3 has a doubled letter in நீர்ககடல், taken for the sea-hued prince's name; the content of Vijayan's words is not given in these lines.
778.event: Vijayan speaks to Tivittan after they reach the desert.

779.reading: The poet says that in the desert the bamboo splits and drops pearls, the rocky ground breathes fire from cracks, and the water the clouds should give is gone.
779.nuance: The desert description is hard to divide into words; the pearl-bamboo and the sense of dried water are read from lines 2 and 3 only roughly.

780.reading: The poet says the tall bamboo ripens and sparks, scattering parched grain over the rocks, which seethe all around.
780.nuance: உக்க நெற்பொரி is taken as parched rice grains fallen from the bamboo; the verse is a picture of heat and the grammar is unsettled.

links.note: In 409 the astrologer reads from the horoscope that within a month Tivittan will split a lion's mouth; in 769 the lion's blood is seen running down the hill.
links.teaches: The prophecy's fulfilment is shown only through its aftermath, the blood stream, so the reader sees the foretold deed by its trace.

links.note: In 446 the priest names the foe's destroyer as the lion-slaying man; 772 shows the deed that gives him that name.
links.teaches: The lion-slaying title that the priest later uses against the rival king is shown being earned here as a protective act.

links.note: Kural 550 likens a king's killing of the cruel to pulling weeds from young corn; verse 772 praises a prince's killing of a beast that preyed on the herds, as a gift of safe sleep to the world.
links.teaches: The epic carries the weeding rule from criminals to a beast, and gives the reason in the world's sleep, though a Jain poet still has to justify a killing.

gains.a: The verse lacks a rule that makes the killing of the cruel a king's care for the many, and so answers why a Jain work may praise it.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a case where the killed is a beast and the killer a prince, which tests how far the weeding image stretches.

links.note: Kural 388 makes the ruler who does justice and protects an இறை for the people; verse 773 sets the king's sons under the same duty and says it outweighs their own lives.
links.teaches: The duty to protect reaches the king's sons and is stated as a willingness to lose their lives, which the couplet leaves unsaid.

gains.a: The verse lacks a status that rewards protection, which the couplet states as being counted an இறை.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the cost of protection, the prince's risk to his life, which the verse names.

links.note: Naladiyar 34 tells one to take the great fruit of a rare body while it lasts; verse 774 says the body yields no fruit if it cannot help the afflicted.
links.teaches: The body's fruit is named as aid to others in trouble, where the quatrain leaves what the fruit is to the word virtue.

gains.a: The verse lacks the impermanence of the body, the cane refuse that makes using it now urgent.
gains.b: The quatrain lacks a concrete form of virtue, the relief of the helpless, that the verse gives it.

links.note: Tirumanthiram 724 keeps the body alive because true knowledge needs a living frame; verse 775 holds that a man should give even himself to end the world's pain.
links.teaches: A Jain epic's praise of the body given away for others and a Saiva text's care for the body to win knowledge set out two uses of the same frame.

gains.a: The verse lacks any limit on self-giving, the claim that the body must be kept for the sake of knowledge.
gains.b: The mantra lacks a counter-ethic, the claim that the body may be spent for another's pain, which tests its practical argument.

links.note: Kural 235 speaks of a death that is really existence, a growth through ruin; verse 776 says the flesh body goes while the form of fame stands.
links.teaches: The verse supplies the two-body picture that explains the couplet's death that is existence, as the fame body that survives.

gains.a: The verse lacks the couplet's claim that only the skilled manage this exchange, which makes the fame body an achievement.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a plain statement of what survives the death, the form of fame, that the verse gives.

source_issues: Verse 767: line 2 had a stray space before a dead consonant, repaired in the core text.
Verse 778: line 3 reads நீர்ககடல் with a doubled letter, taken for the sea-hued prince's epithet.
Verses 758 to 776: the speaker is Vijayan, taken from 767 and 768, where the poet says the conch-hued one showed these sights and spoke; none of these verses names him.
Verse 777 reads தங்கதை, taken as தம் கதை (their mace); doubtful.
